---
title: "3.4 Spatial cross-validation in practice"
---

<!--
  PLACEHOLDER. Drafted from the course outline and the Spring 2027 daily syllabus (Feb 15 session).
  Outline description: "the first time students see how much a spatial split changes their reported
  accuracy." This chapter comes after students have a random forest to evaluate. Replace the italic notes
  with text as each section is written.
-->

When a model is tested on examples that sit right next to its training examples, it is being tested on a problem it has already half seen. Nearby places tend to be similar, so a random split of spatial data can make a model look far better than it will be when it is used somewhere new. This chapter is where you measure how much that matters, by evaluating your own random forest in two ways and comparing the results.

::: {.callout-note title="Learning objectives"}
By the end of this chapter you should be able to

- run random and spatial cross-validation on the same model
- explain why the two give different accuracy, and which one better matches how the model will be used
- map a model's residuals and describe any spatial pattern in its errors
- decide when spatial cross-validation is the right evaluation for a project
:::
